final_recommendation: The room converged on a concrete path: Mexico commits to binding audit text with automatic 45-day tariff suspension (no Mexican veto, single-violation trigger) by Friday; labor confirms this closes their enforcement demand; Congress commits to a floor vote by end of next week. Canada's dairy and Chapter 19 remain untouched. The package moves to ratification as amended.
minority_objections: Labor initially demanded 90-day remediation window instead of 45 days, though ultimately accepted 45 with binding language
Canada repeatedly warned against reopening other chapters (dairy, Chapter 19) if labor enforcement was amended
key_conflicts: Labor vs. Mexico on automatic tariff suspension: labor demanded upfront enforcement threat; Mexico initially rejected as sovereignty violation
Timeline tension: 45-day vs. 90-day remediation window for verified violations
Definition of 'verified violation' and whether Mexico gets cure period before tariff clock starts
Trust deficit: Congress/labor skeptical Mexico would accept binding enforcement; Mexico skeptical U.S. would actually vote after concessions
key_concessions: Mexico accepted automatic tariff suspension on day 45 with zero discretionary escape—major sovereignty concession
Mexico accepted single-violation trigger with no cure window before tariff clock starts
Labor accepted 45-day (not 90-day) remediation window in exchange for binding audit text
Business lobby committed floor support contingent on Friday binding text, accelerating timeline pressure
red_lines: Labor: automatic tariff enforcement with no Mexican veto—'if there's wiggle room on violation definition, we're not there'
Mexico: no U.S. unilateral tariff imposition without Mexico at the table; enforcement must respect Mexican sovereignty
Canada: dairy concession and Chapter 19 cannot be reopened—'my government walks from ratification entirely' if other chapters move
Congress: signed binding text by Friday with no further conditions, or no floor vote
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: whether 45-day window is operationally sufficient for genuine remediation (labor accepted but flagged as 'tight')
Audit definition risk: 'verified violation' definition remained somewhat ambiguous despite assurances
Political risk in Mexico: domestic backlash to accepting automatic U.S. tariff suspension was not discussed
Timeline risk: Friday-to-next-week vote schedule leaves almost no buffer for text disputes or last-minute objections
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Friday's signed audit text actually contains zero wiggle room on violation triggers and tariff automaticity
Whether Congress can actually deliver floor vote by end of next week given caucus dynamics
Whether media narrative shift ('labor enforcement finally works') lands with skeptical House members in time
Whether Mexico's domestic political coalition accepts the sovereignty concession on automatic tariffs
Whether Canada's red line (no reopening other chapters) holds if implementation issues emerge
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved procedural convergence (Friday text, next-week vote) but left operational uncertainties unresolved: exact audit language defining 'verified violation,' whether 45 days is genuinely sufficient for remediation, and whether Mexico's domestic ratification can survive the automatic-tariff concession. The timeline is extremely compressed, leaving almost no margin for text disputes or implementation clarifications.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Drove every exchange: 'votes aren't there without real labor enforcement,' 'dead on arrival,' 'dies in committee'—ratification failure was the central threat forcing all concessions
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Dominated room from start: labor's demand for automatic tariffs with no Mexican veto shaped every round, forced Mexico's major sovereignty concession, and determined final package
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Present and influential (committed floor support contingent on Friday text, accelerated timeline) but secondary to labor-Mexico enforcement standoff
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly intervened to protect dairy/Chapter 19 red line, but this was defensive—not a driving force shaping the labor enforcement compromise
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Central driver: Mexico's sovereignty concern ('Mexico enforces labor law in Mexico') forced negotiation of trilateral mechanisms, but Mexico ultimately conceded automatic tariffs—this tension shaped the entire deal structure
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor consistently framed narrative stakes ('either workers won or got rolled') and pushed Congress to see enforcement as victory, but this was supportive rather than driving the core negotiation
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Explicitly central: room treated ratification as contingent on amendment ('we need to reopen this'), and final convergence required Mexico's binding concession plus Congress vote commitment—stability depended entirely on domestic-ratification compromise
